item.title: ICYMI: Fed’s Jefferson says inflation is the key signal for rates, with PCE still at 3.6%
item.description:
Jefferson’s comments support pricing for a December hike without adding to the half-point tail, which suits the steady, gradual camp. By naming energy as the main channel for broader inflation, he makes Fed expectations sensitive to oil. Any renewed jump in crude tied to the Iran war and Hormuz shipping risk would feed quickly into rate pricing and the US dollar. His upbeat view on growth and jobs also removes an easy reason to pause. That keeps front-end Treasury yields supported, and continues to put gold under pressure from the Fed’s tightening path.

---

With unemployment steady and growth near potential, Jefferson has made it plain that inflation, and energy-driven inflation in particular, now sets the Fed’s course.

Summary:

  • Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson said the trajectory of inflation is the most important signal for setting monetary policy.
  • He said further moves should depend on data trends, the outlook and the balance of risks.
  • Headline PCE inflation was 3.6% in September and core PCE was 3.1%. October data so far shows pressures staying well above target.
  • He is concerned that higher energy prices could cause a broader, persistent rise in inflation, already visible in airfares and transport.
  • Unemployment was 4.1% in October, which he sees as consistent with maximum employment. Q3 GDP grew at an annualised 3.4%.
  • He voted with the majority to hold rates in October.

Federal Reserve Vice Chair Philip Jefferson said the path of inflation, rather than growth or jobs, will be the main guide for future interest rate decisions, as price pressures remain well above the central bank’s 2% target.

Speaking at the University of California, San Diego Economic Roundtable on Friday, Jefferson said further policy moves should be decided by carefully weighing trends in the data, the changing outlook and the balance of risks, ANI reported. He described inflation’s trajectory as the more important signal for setting the stance of policy.

Figures cited in his speech showed headline personal consumption expenditures inflation at 3.6% in September, with core PCE, which strips out food and energy, at 3.1%. Jefferson said the October inflation data received so far point to price pressures staying well above target.

He flagged energy as the main risk. Jefferson said he remains concerned that higher energy prices could lead to a broader and more persistent rise in inflation, noting that the effect is already visible in airfares and transport costs. Strong demand for new technologies is also lifting prices of some goods, including memory chips.

By contrast, his assessment of the real economy was steady. Jefferson said labour market conditions have stabilised, with unemployment at 4.1% in October, a level he regards as consistent with maximum employment and expects to hold in the near term. The economy has gained momentum this year, he said, with third-quarter GDP growing at an annualised 3.4%, roughly in line with its potential.

Jefferson said he voted with the majority to hold rates at the Federal Open Market Committee’s October meeting. Since then, he said, activity and the labour market have remained broadly solid, while inflation readings have continued to show persistent pressure.

As vice chair, Jefferson’s views carry weight with the committee’s centre. By putting inflation ahead of a stable labour market, his remarks fit the Fed’s tightening bias, with markets widely expecting a quarter-point rate increase at the December meeting. Upcoming core PCE data will be a key test of that view. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Weekend: Bessent urges Nvidia to hire an outsider CEO, pouring cold water on a Huang comeback
item.description:
Bessent’s comments make Nvidia’s leadership question a political one. With a cabinet official openly favouring an outside hire, a Huang return becomes harder for the board to justify, and the recent rally in comeback hopes looks fragile. The 10-day deadline puts a near-term overhang on the stock beyond Tuesday’s results, since any finding that sales to China-linked shell companies were knowingly pursued could bring penalties or tighter export curbs. His opposition to new legislation offers chip stocks some relief, but bipartisan momentum in Congress means export-control risk is still high for the wider semiconductor sector.

---

Just as Huang’s allies were building a comeback campaign, Washington weighed in: the Treasury Secretary wants an outsider in charge and answers on Nvidia’s China sales within 10 days.

Summary:

  • Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Nvidia needs a dramatic leadership shakeup and should look outside the company for its next CEO.
  • His remarks came as Jensen Huang was reported to be discussing a return, backed by Silicon Valley allies.
  • Bessent wants to know whether Nvidia ignored warning signs that shell companies, many in Singapore, were funnelling its AI chips to China.
  • He said the board and its outside counsel should provide answers within the next 10 days.
  • He opposed new legislation to lock in chip export controls, saying existing rules need enforcing.
  • Nvidia shares fell about 12.5% last week. Interim CEO Colette Kress presents results on Tuesday.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Nvidia needs a “dramatic shakeup” in its leadership and should look outside the company for its next chief executive. His comments push directly against reports that ousted CEO Jensen Huang is weighing a comeback.

Speaking on Fox News’s Sunday Morning Futures, Bessent said the allegations surrounding the chipmaker suggest the board should hire from outside as it searches for a new leader. His comments came on the same day the Financial Times reported that Huang has been discussing a return, with Silicon Valley allies assembling a “war room” to build support. Nvidia and a Huang spokesperson declined to comment to the newspaper.

Bessent tried to shift the focus away from Huang’s personal conduct and toward legal and national security questions. He said he wants to know whether Nvidia knowingly ignored warning signs that shell companies, many based in Singapore, were channelling its advanced AI chips to China, and whether the company pushed such sales to lift revenue and earnings. He said the board and its outside counsel should provide answers within the next 10 days.

Huang stepped down on Thursday after revelations of an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed International whom US officials suspect of spying for China. Bessent said he had long backed adding Megaspeed to a trade blacklist, but noted that the decision rested with the Commerce Department.

The Treasury chief also pushed back on calls in Congress for legislation to lock in chip export restrictions. He argued that existing rules are sufficient and simply need to be enforced. Lawmakers from both parties are backing a bill that could pass within weeks.

Bessent’s comments raise the stakes for Nvidia’s board ahead of quarterly results on Tuesday, which interim chief executive Colette Kress will present. Nvidia shares fell about 12.5% last week. Huang has agreed to testify before lawmakers behind closed doors. The board’s handling of both the succession and the compliance review will now be watched closely in Washington as well as on Wall Street. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6771 – Reuters estimate
item.description:
The People’s Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day’s closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point. A stronger-than-expected CNY midpoint is typically read as a sign the PBOC is leaning against depreciation pressure, while a weaker fixing for the CNY can indicate tolerance for a softer currency, often in response to dollar strength or domestic economic headwinds.In periods of heightened global volatility, such as shifts in US rate expectations, trade tensions or capital flow pressures, the fixing takes on added significance. For investors, it provides insight into Beijing’s currency priorities, balancing competitiveness, capital stability and financial market confidence.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Japan Q3 GDP shrinks 0.1% annualised vs +0.3% expected as exports and consumers weigh
item.description:
A flat quarter made weak mainly by trade is unlikely to derail BoJ tightening plans by itself. Strong capex and positive domestic demand are the parts policymakers watch most closely. The miss still gives the yen little help just as USD/JPY presses toward 160, and that raises the stakes for any comments from Japanese officials on the currency. JGB yields may ease slightly at the front end if traders trim December hike bets. The bigger driver for the session is Takata’s speech later today, where a hawkish response to the data would quickly restore conviction. For the Nikkei, softer growth and a weak yen are a familiar, broadly supportive mix for exporters.

---

Earlier preivew:

  • Economic and event calendar in Asia, Monday, November 16, 2026. BoJ, China data, Japan GDP.

---

Japan’s Q3 stall was a trade story more than a domestic one: exports and cautious shoppers dragged, but strong business investment leaves the BoJ’s December hike case largely intact.

Summary:

  • Japan’s preliminary Q3 GDP contracted an annualised 0.1%, against forecasts of +0.3% growth and following +1.4% in Q2.
  • Quarter on quarter, GDP was flat at 0.0%, versus a forecast of +0.1% and +0.4% previously.
  • External demand subtracted 0.6 percentage point (forecast -0.4), and exports fell 0.2% q/q.
  • Private consumption fell 0.3% q/q, against a forecast of a 0.2% decline.
  • Capex rose 1.6% q/q, beating the 1.5% forecast after a 0.9% drop in Q2. Domestic demand added 0.6 point.
  • The GDP deflator rose 2.4% y/y, below the 2.6% forecast and the previous 2.6%.

Japan’s economy stalled in the July to September quarter. Preliminary data showed real GDP contracted at an annualised 0.1%, short of the 0.3% growth economists had expected and a sharp slowdown from 1.4% in the second quarter. On a quarterly basis, output was flat, against a forecast of a 0.1% gain.

The miss came from two places. External demand subtracted 0.6 percentage point from growth, more than the 0.4 point drag expected, with exports slipping 0.2% from the previous quarter. Private consumption, which accounts for more than half of the economy, fell 0.3%, a slightly deeper drop than the 0.2% decline forecast.

Business investment was the bright spot. Capital expenditure jumped 1.6% from the prior quarter, just ahead of expectations of 1.5%, and reversed a 0.9% fall in the April to June period. Overall, domestic demand added 0.6 percentage point to growth, which shows the weakness was concentrated in trade rather than in the domestic economy as a whole.

Price pressure across the economy also came in a little softer. The GDP deflator, a broad measure of prices across the economy, rose 2.4% from a year earlier, below forecasts and the previous quarter’s 2.6%, though still comfortably above the Bank of Japan’s 2% target.

The figures land at a sensitive moment for the BoJ, which held its policy rate at 1.25% in October and is widely expected to raise it to 1.5% in December. A flat quarter driven by trade, alongside firm capital spending and positive domestic demand, gives policymakers grounds to look through the headline number. The softer consumption reading, however, will give more cautious board members something to point to.

Attention now turns to BoJ board member Hajime Takata, who speaks later on Monday at 04:00 GMT (11:00 pm ET Sunday). Takata has dissented at recent meetings in favour of faster tightening, and his read on the data will be watched for any shift in the December debate. A revised GDP estimate is due next month and could change the picture if the capex or consumption figures are updated. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: US futures open firmer as Nasdaq leads, oil slips despite Iran tanker claims: 5 things
item.description:
The opening tone is cautiously risk-on, but thin early liquidity means these moves are a tentative read rather than a settled direction. Oil’s restraint is the notable signal. With three US carrier groups now in the region and Iran claiming more mine strikes, the risk premium is skewed upward if any tanker sinking is independently confirmed, so dips in crude look vulnerable to headline risk. In FX, USD/JPY is pressing toward 160, which keeps yen intervention risk alive just as Japanese GDP lands and BoJ hawk Takata speaks later in the session. Gold remains caught between geopolitical tension and a Fed on a hiking path, and the hiking path is winning for now.

---

Futures have shrugged off a weekend of Iranian tanker claims, Nvidia leadership drama and hawkish Fed talk, with tech leading the early bid and oil waiting for proof before it reacts.

Summary:

  • S&P 500 futures rose about 0.3% and Nasdaq 100 futures gained around 0.6% at the weekly open.

US stock index futures opened the new week on the front foot in early Asia-Pacific trade on Monday, led by technology. Oil prices edged lower even after Iran claimed fresh mine strikes on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz over the weekend. Prices below are as of around 23:40 GMT (6:40 pm ET on Sunday).

Signs of strain in AI financing are also worth watching, after Blackstone-backed data center operator QTS cut a planned debt sale by about 60%.

Separately, the USS Theodore Roosevelt has reportedly arrived in the Middle East. It joins the USS George H.W. Bush and USS George Washington, giving the US three carrier strike groups in the region.

Gold Gold was little changed around $3,890 an ounce, with hawkish Fed commentary over the weekend keeping a lid on gains.

Bitcoin Bitcoin rose nearly 2% to around $65,300, outperforming other risk assets in early trade.

What’s ahead The Fed is widely expected to raise rates by a quarter point at its December 8-9 meeting. item.title: ECB bond market intervention warning from Governor Knot. Can’t replace sound fiscal policy,
item.description:
Knot’s line on fiscal discipline matters most for euro zone sovereign spreads, especially French bonds against German Bunds. Markets will read it as a reminder that ECB support would be conditional rather than open-ended. A president with that view could make investors less willing to bet on a full central bank backstop if French finances get worse, which risks wider spreads during periods of stress. On rates, his cautious, data-driven stance on energy-driven inflation is softer than the hike signals coming from more hawkish policymakers, so a Knot presidency would lean toward patience rather than front-loaded tightening. The leadership race is now a live factor for the euro and for periphery bonds.

---

Knot is pitching himself as an ECB chief who will steady bond markets in a crisis but won’t bail out lax budgets, a message aimed at Paris as much as at the markets.

Summary:

  • Former Dutch central bank governor Klaas Knot said ECB bond-market interventions cannot replace responsible fiscal policy.
  • He said the ECB can act to stabilise disorderly sovereign bond trading, but that is no substitute for sustainable public finances.
  • Concerns about France’s public finances have revived fears of another euro zone debt crisis.
  • Knot is competing with Pablo Hernandez de Cos to succeed Christine Lagarde, who leaves on February 7.
  • He backed a cautious, data-driven approach on rates. The Iran war has lifted energy prices, but there is limited evidence of second-round effects.
  • He cited resilient demand, strong employment, defence spending and US AI investment as supports for European growth.

The European Central Bank can step into government bond markets to restore order when trading turns disorderly, but it cannot take the place of responsible public spending and debt management. Former Dutch central bank governor Klaas Knot made the point as he campaigns to become the ECB’s next president.

His remarks carry particular weight because worries over France’s public finances have revived talk of a fresh euro zone debt crisis, putting a spotlight on how far the central bank would go to contain market stress. By drawing a clear line between short-term stabilisation and long-term fiscal discipline, Knot signalled that any ECB backstop would come with expectations for governments attached.

Knot is competing with former Spanish central bank governor Pablo Hernandez de Cos to succeed Christine Lagarde, who said last month she would step down on February 7, roughly nine months before her term ends. Whoever wins will inherit a structural challenge: 21 euro zone governments set their own fiscal policies, which makes coordination with a single monetary policy harder.

On the economy, Knot struck a broadly upbeat tone. He pointed to resilient domestic demand, a strong labour market and healthy private-sector balance sheets. He also highlighted higher defence spending and US investment in artificial intelligence as further sources of activity that benefit Europe.

On inflation, he urged caution. He acknowledged that the Iran war has pushed up energy prices and added to near-term inflation pressure. He said the key unknown is whether higher energy costs feed through into wages and wider consumer prices. With inflation expectations broadly stable and little evidence so far of widespread second-round effects, he backed a measured approach, saying policymakers should stay flexible and let incoming data guide future rate decisions.

Knot also said his thinking on monetary policy has changed since the earlier debt crisis, when persistently low inflation split northern and southern policymakers. That shift could matter for how governments in the south see him.

The next ECB president will have to balance price stability against the risk of financial instability, at a time when geopolitical tensions and government borrowing are clouding the euro zone outlook. 

French bond spreads have only been one part of this story. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Trump out of public view since Wednesday, fuelling speculation on his wherabouts
item.description:
For markets, this is a non-event as long as the official record keeps showing normal activity. Traders have learned to discount social media speculation about the president’s health, and nothing so far has moved oil, Treasuries or the US dollar on this story. The risk lies in his travel plans. A smooth departure for China would close the story, but an unexplained delay or cancellation would quickly become a factor for markets. With the Iran war still shaping energy prices, any real uncertainty at the top would tend to lift oil’s risk premium and support safe-haven demand for the dollar.

---

Trump’s few days out of view have set off the usual online rumours, but the documented record shows a president working behind closed doors, and an expected trip to China this week should put him back in front of the cameras.

Summary:

  • Trump has not made a public appearance since Wednesday. His last sighting was a privately recorded White House interview on Thursday.
  • The White House called a travel and photo lid on Saturday, a routine notice that the president won’t be seen.
  • His Sunday schedule showed a full day of calls and meetings, and he posted that he was working at the White House. Calendar entries also show a visit to his golf club.
  • He has not publicly addressed Friday’s nationwide FAA ground stop, which cabinet officials have handled.
  • Speculation online about his health has no supporting evidence in the public record.
  • Trump is expected to travel to China for the APEC summit on November 18-19.

President Donald Trump has not made a public appearance since Wednesday, a gap that has stirred online speculation about his whereabouts. However, the official record of his activity over that period points to a president working out of view rather than one who is absent.

The most recent sighting came on Thursday, when Trump recorded a video interview with sports commentator Stephen A. Smith inside the White House. On Saturday the White House called a travel and photo lid, the routine notice that the president will not be seen publicly that day. On Sunday, his published schedule showed him working from early morning until late evening on calls and meetings, and Trump posted on Truth Social that he was at the White House holding meetings on a range of subjects. Calendar entries also record a Sunday visit to his golf club and his return.

The low profile has drawn attention largely because it overlapped with Friday’s nationwide FAA ground stop, which Trump has not addressed in public. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has linked that disruption to faulty work on a telecom systems upgrade at a remote site, and the response so far has been led by cabinet officials.

Some social media accounts have gone further, suggesting without evidence that the president is unwell or worse. Nothing in the public record supports that. Scrutiny of the schedule has run well ahead of the evidence, and the documented calendar, posts and official accounts describe his movements rather than any change in his health.

Short absences like this are not new. Trump went about a week without a public appearance in late May and early June before returning to announce an executive order from the Oval Office. In April, during a similar quiet spell in the Iran war, the White House said he was working nonstop.

The next clear test is his travel this week. Trump is expected to go to China for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, scheduled for November 18 and 19 in Shenzhen, which would put him back in front of cameras within days.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Weekend - Blackstone’s QTS cuts AI data center debt sale 60% as investors push back on pricing
item.description:
For credit markets, the QTS cutback is an early sign that the price of financing AI infrastructure is starting to matter. Investors are putting limits on how much they will hold of repeat issuers and on concentrated exposure to the sector. If that spreads, data center and AI-linked borrowers could face wider spreads or smaller deals, pushing more issuance into private credit and project finance at higher cost. For equities, any rise in funding costs feeds into the capex economics behind the AI trade. That is a sensitive point for sentiment this week, with Nvidia due to report on Tuesday. The deal is small, so it is not a credit event, but it is a signal worth tracking in future AI debt deals.

---

Big week for AI ahead:

  • Anthropic IPO six times oversubscribed: what retail investors can realistically expect

---

The AI build-out has had seemingly unlimited access to capital, but QTS’s shrunken deal shows that even a Blackstone-backed borrower now has to choose between paying up and settling for less.

Summary:

  • QTS, a Blackstone-backed data center operator, cut a planned private debt sale by about 60%.
  • It is raising about $300 million, down from an initial target of roughly $800 million.
  • Some investors objected to pricing, while others were limited by QTS’s repeated use of the private placement market.
  • QTS has raised billions through at least two private placements in 18 months, including a $1.65 billion high-grade sale last year.
  • Blackstone resisted higher yields because wider pricing could become a costlier benchmark for its other debt.
  • AI companies are tapping every part of the capital markets to fund investment that could reach the trillions of dollars.

QTS, the data center operator backed by Blackstone, has scaled back a planned private debt sale by around 60% after struggling to find enough investor demand, and after declining to pay the much higher yields some buyers wanted, Bloomberg reported, citing people familiar with the transaction.

The company is now raising about $300 million, down from an initial target of roughly $800 million. Some investors objected to the pricing on offer, while others were constrained because QTS has already tapped the private placement market several times, according to the people.

QTS has been a heavy user of that market. It has raised billions of dollars through at least two private placement deals over the past 18 months, including a $1.65 billion high-grade bond sale last year and a separate $800 million financing.

Blackstone’s reluctance to sweeten terms reflects a wider concern. Because the firm borrows frequently across many markets and through many issuers, wider pricing on the QTS deal could set a more expensive benchmark for investors weighing other Blackstone-related debt.

The episode matters well beyond one borrower. Artificial intelligence companies are reaching into every corner of capital markets, from investment-grade bonds to project finance, to fund build-outs that could cost trillions of dollars over the coming years. The QTS deal suggests that appetite is not unlimited, particularly in narrower pools such as private placements, where a small group of buyers can quickly hit internal limits on exposure to a single name or sector.

That leaves borrowers with an uncomfortable choice: accept higher funding costs, shrink deals or spread issuance across more markets. Each option raises the cost or complexity of financing the AI infrastructure boom. For now, the decision to cut the deal’s size rather than pay up shows that well-backed issuers can still walk away. But it is a sign that the market is starting to discriminate on price.

The next test will be how other data center and AI-related borrowers do in upcoming deals, and whether investors start demanding a premium for concentrated exposure to the sector.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: ICYMI - Trump extends Jones Act waiver 90 days, foreign tankers moving oil in US
item.description:
For oil, the extension is a small but useful relief valve rather than a supply story. It does not add barrels to the market, but it moves them more efficiently between US regions. That should help limit regional price spikes in gasoline and diesel, particularly on the East and West coasts, which depend on waterborne deliveries. The fact that most of the extra volume has been refined products suggests the main effect is on product cracks and regional spreads rather than on benchmark crude. Since the administration is still relying on emergency measures like this, traders should take it as a sign that Washington does not expect fuel prices tied to the Iran war to ease soon.

---

Earlier:

  • Iran says supertanker with 2 million barrels sank after Hormuz mine strike, unconfirmed

---

Washington has again set aside a century-old shipping protection in the name of cheaper fuel, a sign that the Iran war’s pressure on gasoline and diesel prices is still running ahead of political sensitivities over shipbuilding.

Summary:

  • President Trump extended a waiver of the Jones Act for 90 days, letting foreign-flagged ships carry oil and commodities between US ports.
  • It is already the longest waiver in the history of the more than 100-year-old law.
  • A blanket waiver was issued in March, a month after the US launched the war on Iran. It moved to case-by-case approval in August, which continues.
  • The White House says around 90 million extra barrels of petroleum, mostly refined, have moved between US ports since March.
  • That includes roughly 27 million barrels of gasoline, 26 million of crude and 6 million of renewable fuels.
  • Waivers have traditionally been kept short because of the domestic shipbuilding lobby.

President Donald Trump has extended a waiver of the Jones Act for a further 90 days, allowing foreign-flagged vessels to keep moving oil and other commodities between US ports as Washington tries to contain fuel costs pushed higher by the war on Iran. Reuters reported the extension on Friday, citing a White House official.

Industry sources had flagged the decision a day earlier. The extension keeps in place what is already the longest waiver in the century-old law’s history.

The Jones Act requires cargo shipped between US ports to travel on vessels that are US-built, US-owned and crewed by American workers. Suspending it widens the pool of available ships, with the aim of easing transport bottlenecks and lowering prices for gasoline, diesel and fertiliser.

The administration first issued a blanket waiver in March, a month after the US launched the war on Iran. When it extended the waiver in August, the White House moved to case-by-case approvals, and that condition carries over into the latest extension.

According to the White House, around 90 million additional barrels of petroleum, mostly refined products, have moved between US ports since the waiver took effect. That includes roughly 27 million barrels of gasoline, 26 million barrels of crude and 6 million barrels of renewable fuels.

Jones Act waivers have historically been kept short because the law has strong backing from the domestic shipbuilding industry, an influential lobby across the country. That makes the length of the current waiver notable, and a sign of how much weight the administration is putting on fuel affordability while the conflict continues.

The extension runs for another three months, which takes it into the northern winter, when demand for heating fuel and distillates usually rises. Whether it is renewed again is likely to depend on how the war and energy prices develop, and on how much pushback the administration faces from the shipbuilding lobby. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Iran says supertanker with 2 million barrels sank after Hormuz mine strike, unconfirmed
item.description:
Oil is the main channel for this news. A claimed sinking of a fully laden supertanker in the world’s most important crude chokepoint is likely to add to the risk premium in Brent and WTI when markets reopen (futures at 6pm Sunday, US Eastern time), even without independent confirmation. The bigger risk is about behaviour rather than barrels. If shipowners conclude that the US-cleared lanes and covert transits are not safe, Hormuz flows could shrink further, and freight rates and war-risk insurance costs could climb. If the claims are not confirmed, or are shown to be overstated, part of any initial jump could fade quickly, given how many similar Iranian announcements markets have already absorbed.

---

Friday news ICYMI:

  • Iran’s Guards claim strike on US radar in Bahrain, warn firms over Hormuz oil trade

---

Iran says its mines have sunk a laden supertanker in the Gulf, a claim no one else has yet confirmed, but its warning to ships using unapproved Hormuz routes is aimed squarely at oil markets and shipowners.

Summary:

  • Iran’s IRGC Navy said two tankers with transponders off hit mines on an unauthorised route in the southern Strait of Hormuz.
  • It said a supertanker carrying more than 2 million barrels of crude sank in the southern Gulf, and the second tanker was still on fire.
  • Iran’s regular Army Navy described a single tanker hitting a mine and catching fire in a prohibited zone east of the strait.
  • Neither account named the vessels or their flags, and there was no independent confirmation.
  • A UK maritime monitor was aware of a separate report of a tanker attack in the Gulf, but could not link it to the Iranian claims.
  • Iran warned ships against passage without its armed forces’ coordination, and against what it called US-backed covert transits.

Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said on Sunday that two oil tankers struck naval mines while using what Tehran calls an unauthorised route through the Strait of Hormuz. They said one of them, a supertanker carrying more than 2 million barrels of crude, sank in the southern Gulf. There was no independent confirmation of either incident.

In a statement carried by Iranian state television, the IRGC Navy said both vessels had their transponders switched off. It said the second tanker was still burning, and warned other ships against what it called US-backed covert passage and deception. The Guards did not disclose the names or flags of the vessels, and there was no information on the crews.

A separate statement from Iran’s regular Army Navy gave a narrower account. It described a single tanker, operating with its navigation systems off in a prohibited zone east of the strait, that hit a mine and caught fire. It said any passage not coordinated with Iran’s armed forces would lead to mine strikes and fires. The two accounts differ on the number of ships, the location and whether a vessel sank, and it is unclear whether they describe the same events.

The UK Maritime Trade Operations centre said it was aware of a report from Indian shipping authorities of an attack on a tanker in the Gulf, but could not say whether it was the same incident.

The claims follow a series of similar announcements from Tehran in recent weeks, often blaming mines for ship fires in the strait. Iran has restricted traffic through the waterway and insists that vessels use routes it has authorised. The US military has said it has cleared mines from the main shipping lanes, and the US has imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports.

If confirmed, the sinking of a fully laden supertanker would be one of the most serious shipping losses of the conflict so far, both for the crude lost and for the signal it sends to shipowners and insurers. Confirmation from shipping monitors, the identity of the vessels and any US response will decide how far the episode escalates. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: ECB’s Nagel says another rate hike ‘highly probable’ as energy prices push inflation
item.description:
An explicit signal from the Bundesbank president that further tightening is likely should support the euro and push up short-dated euro zone yields, especially German two-year debt. Because he ties the risk directly to gas and electricity, euro zone rate pricing is now more sensitive to moves in energy markets, so a rise in oil or gas could feed quickly into ECB hike expectations. His comment that the economy has proved resilient also weakens the argument that growth worries will hold the ECB back, which leaves rate-sensitive European equities more exposed.

---

Not only open mouths at the ECB:

  • Weekend Fed speak: Collins backs steady, gradual rate hikes, cool on a bigger December move
  • Sunday Fed talk: Schmid says inflation would still be near 3% without energy, Fed has work to do

----

Nagel has made it clear that the ECB is not finished: with energy prices running ahead of forecasts and expectations creeping higher, Germany’s central bank chief sees another hike as the likely price of avoiding a 2022 rerun.

Summary:

  • Joachim Nagel, ECB Governing Council member and Bundesbank president, said it is highly probable the ECB will have to raise rates again if conditions do not change.
  • He warned that every month of elevated inflation raises the risk of second-round effects.
  • Energy prices have moved well above the path in the September projections, pushing the outlook toward the adverse scenario.
  • Gas and electricity prices have gathered momentum, and early-stage pricing points to more upward pressure.
  • Underlying inflation remains elevated, and short-term inflation expectations have risen with headline inflation.
  • Nagel said the economy has been resilient and a repeat of 2022 is unlikely, as long as the ECB does its job.

European Central Bank policymaker Joachim Nagel said on Friday that the ECB will very likely have to raise borrowing costs again, warning that energy-driven inflation pressures are building faster than the central bank had expected.

If conditions stay as they are, it seems “highly probable” that the ECB will need to act again, the Bundesbank president said in a speech, Bloomberg (gated) reported. He warned that each additional month of elevated inflation increases the risk of second-round effects, where higher prices feed into wages and broader price-setting.

Nagel said the inflation outlook has deteriorated since the ECB’s September projections. That baseline had inflation peaking around the turn of the year and staying above target well into 2027. Since then, he said, energy prices have moved well above the assumed path, and the economy is now approaching the adverse scenario set out in those projections.

He pointed to several sources of pressure. Gas and electricity prices have gathered momentum in recent weeks, and the early stages of the pricing chain point to further increases. Underlying inflation remains elevated, and short-term inflation expectations have risen alongside the jump in headline inflation.

Nagel also noted that the euro zone economy has so far proved resilient. That suggests he sees room to tighten without undermining growth. His remarks frame the policy question around the risk that an energy shock becomes entrenched, rather than around the strength of demand.

He offered some reassurance on the longer view, saying the Bundesbank’s analysis suggests a repeat of the 2022 inflation surge is unlikely, provided the ECB does its job. That condition matters. In his view, avoiding a 2022-style episode depends on the central bank responding in time, rather than waiting for energy prices to ease on their own.

As one of the more influential voices on the Governing Council, Nagel has added weight to expectations of further tightening. The next things to watch are energy prices, how much of them passes through to core inflation, and whether other policymakers share his view that the adverse scenario is becoming more likely.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: New Zealand services PSI hits 3.5-year high at 51.7, fifth straight month of growth
item.description:
A services reading at a multi-year high, led by new orders, strengthens the case that New Zealand’s recovery is spreading beyond a handful of sectors. That gives the New Zealand dollar modest support on the domestic data front. For rate expectations, firmer activity reduces the pressure for further policy support. The flat employment reading and persistent cost-of-living complaints, however, point to slack that has not yet closed. Traders are likely to treat the data as a confidence builder rather than a game changer, and will look to the next few releases to see whether spending held back during the election starts to come through.

---

Also:

  • NZ manufacturing PMI eases to 54.9 in October but extends expansion run to 16 months

---

New Zealand’s services firms are finally seeing new business arrive in volume heading into summer, but with hiring still flat, October’s strength looks more like a pre-Christmas lift than a recovery that has fully taken hold.

Summary:

  • New Zealand’s services PSI rose to 51.7 in October from 50.9, the highest reading in more than three and a half years.
  • It is the fifth consecutive month above the 50 breakeven level.
  • New orders (53.0), activity and sales (52.6) and supplier deliveries (52.1) led the gains.
  • Employment dipped to 49.9, the only sub-index in contraction, and inventories eased to 50.1.
  • The share of negative survey comments fell to 57.9% from 59.9%. Fuel prices, cost of living, interest rates and the election were still the main concerns.
  • Survey comments pointed to summer, Christmas bookings and returning tourists as positives, with hopes that spending deferred during the election will come through.

New Zealand’s services sector expanded for a fifth consecutive month in October, with the BNZ-BusinessNZ Performance of Services Index climbing to 51.7 from 50.9 in September. That is the strongest reading in more than three and a half years. A reading above 50 signals expansion.

The gain was led by forward-looking measures. New orders and business rose to 53.0, activity and sales reached 52.6, and supplier deliveries came in at 52.1. Employment was the only sub-index in contraction, edging just below breakeven at 49.9, and stocks and inventories eased to 50.1.

BusinessNZ chief executive Katherine Rich said the run of readings above breakeven stood out against the past few years. She said it was encouraging to see activity and new business rising together heading into summer. She suggested that many firms had put decisions on hold before the election, and that some of that delayed spending and investment could start to come through by the end of the year once a new government is formed.

Survey comments showed businesses are still preoccupied by fuel prices, the cost of living, interest rates and election uncertainty. On the positive side, respondents pointed to the run-in to summer, Christmas bookings and the return of tourists. The share of negative comments fell to 57.9% from 59.9% in September, a modest improvement in tone.

Economists said firmer services activity is especially welcome because of the sector’s weight in the New Zealand economy and its importance for the GDP outlook. If the improvement holds, they said, it would add to evidence that the recovery is broadening and becoming more established.

The softness in hiring is the main caveat. Firms appear willing to take on new business but are not yet adding staff. The next few months will show whether the election delay was the main drag on investment and jobs, or whether the caution runs deeper.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Weekend Fed speak: Collins backs steady, gradual rate hikes, cool on a bigger December move
item.description:
Collins’s comments push back on the half-point talk that has built since Waller’s remarks and last week’s inflation data. That could trim some of the tail pricing for a larger December move and take a little heat out of the front end of the Treasury curve. Her view that the eventual rate path may be higher cuts the other way, though. It supports the idea of a longer hiking cycle, which keeps the US dollar supported on dips and leaves gold without a clear dovish tailwind. For traders, her message is about the pace of hikes, not when they stop.

---

Also:

  • Sunday Fed talk: Schmid says inflation would still be near 3% without energy, Fed has work to do

---

Collins wants the Fed to keep hiking in small steps rather than speed up, but her admission that the destination may be higher means a gentler pace should not be confused with a softer stance.

Summary:

  • Boston Fed President Susan Collins favours continuing to raise rates at a steady, modest pace, while remaining open-minded.
  • She sees two-sided risks: inflation is high and broadening, the job market is stable and could accelerate, and further shocks remain possible.
  • Higher medium and longer-term rates since the start of the year may weigh on demand more than she expects.
  • She argued against shifting to a more aggressive pace of hikes, and said gradual does not mean a fixed cadence.
  • Recent price data and a firmer labour market suggest the policy rate path over the next year may be higher than she thought.
  • The Fed is widely expected to lift its 3.75% to 4% range by a quarter point on December 8-9, with another rise expected in January.

Boston Federal Reserve President Susan Collins said on Saturday she favours continuing to raise interest rates at a steady, modest pace, arguing that a gradual approach is the better way to handle the uncertainties facing the US economy, Reuters reported.

Speaking to reporters at a housing conference hosted by her bank in Boston, Collins said “a steady, gradual path” of tightening looked right to her for now, though she stressed she remained open-minded. She also cautioned that a gradual approach does not necessarily mean a set rhythm of moves.

Collins described the risks to the real economy as two-sided. On one side, inflation is high and price gains are spreading more widely through the economy, while the job market is stable and could pick up. On the other, the economy is still exposed to further shocks, and the rise in medium and longer-term borrowing costs since the start of the year may restrain demand more than she currently assumes.

Taken together, she said, those factors argue against the Fed stepping up to a more aggressive pace of increases, even though inflation has run above the 2% target for more than five years.

Her comments matter because the debate inside the Fed has shifted from whether to hike to how fast. The Fed last lifted rates in September and is widely expected to raise its 3.75% to 4% target range by a quarter point at the December 8-9 meeting, followed by another increase in January. Most officials have signalled support for small, steady moves, partly to give the economy time to absorb higher borrowing costs. However, recent inflation data and comments from Governor Christopher Waller have raised the possibility that some policymakers want a larger step next month.

Collins did not argue for less tightening overall. She said the past three months of price data, together with a firmer labour market, have led her to think the path of policy rates over the next year may end up somewhat higher than she expected a couple of months ago. Her preference is about pace rather than destination, which leaves the door open to more tightening, delivered in smaller steps.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Sunday Fed talk: Schmid says inflation would still be near 3% without energy, Fed has work to do
item.description:
Schmid’s remarks add weight to hike pricing that is already in place for December. His attack on the “supply shock” argument also makes it harder to make the dovish case for looking through energy-driven inflation. That supports the US dollar and front-end Treasury yields, and it keeps the small tail risk of a half-point move alive. A Fed seen as committed to further tightening has been a headwind for gold throughout this cycle. His view that AI-driven demand will respond to higher rates is also a reminder to rate-sensitive tech valuations that the sector is not exempt from policy.

---

Schmid stopped short of calling for a hike, but he took apart both main arguments that inflation is beyond the Fed’s control, leaving little room for the doves ahead of December.

Summary:

  • Kansas City Fed President Jeff Schmid said inflation is running too hot, uncomfortably above the 2% target and moving in the wrong direction.
  • He said inflation would still be around 3% with energy prices excluded.
  • He rejected views that supply shocks, or AI-driven demand that is resistant to rates, put inflation beyond the Fed’s reach.
  • He said the labour market is broadly in balance, with little evidence that wages are adding to inflation.
  • He did not specifically call for more hikes. Markets are fully priced for a quarter-point rise in December.
  • Schmid is not a voting member of the FOMC this year.

Kansas City Federal Reserve President Jeff Schmid said on Sunday that US inflation is running too hot and that the Fed still has work to do to bring it under control. He pushed back against arguments that current price pressures are beyond the central bank’s reach.

Speaking to a credit union conference in Hawaii, Schmid said inflation is uncomfortably above the Fed’s 2% target and moving in the wrong direction, Reuters reported. He noted that inflation would still be running at about 3% even with energy prices stripped out, which suggests the problem is broader than the oil shock. He did not specifically call for further rate increases.

The core of his remarks was a rebuttal of two narratives that have gained ground recently. The first holds that high inflation reflects a run of supply shocks the Fed cannot fix. Schmid’s view is that inflation always comes from an imbalance between supply and demand, and that supply disruptions push prices higher precisely because demand is strong. Because the Fed influences demand, he argued, it always has both the tools and the responsibility to respond.

The second narrative holds that the current sources of demand, such as the artificial intelligence buildout, are resistant to higher interest rates. Schmid disagreed. He also rejected the idea that meeting the inflation goal requires prices in any single category, such as AI-related technology goods, to respond. In his view, it is not the Fed’s role to target the price of any one good or service.

Schmid described the labour market as broadly in balance, with little sign that jobs or wages are adding to inflation. He also echoed Chair Kevin Warsh, saying the work of containing inflation has only become harder since Warsh’s Jackson Hole speech.

Schmid is not a voting member of the policy-setting committee this year. The Fed raised rates by a quarter point in September to a 3.75% to 4.00% range, then held at its October meeting. Inflation data has since come in hotter than expected, and other officials, including Governor Christopher Waller, have also spoken. Futures markets are now fully priced for a quarter-point increase in December, with a small chance of a half-point move. Schmid’s comments add to the chorus arguing that the hiking cycle is not yet finished.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Jensen Huang weighs Nvidia comeback days after quitting over scandal, FT reports
item.description:
The comeback talk adds a new layer of uncertainty to Nvidia shares going into Tuesday’s results, and traders now have two outcomes to price: an outside successor or a return of the founder. A Huang return could ease worries about execution during the product ramp, but it would bring back regulatory and China-export risk while US inquiries are still open. Because Nvidia’s weighting is so large, any swing in its shares on the leadership news is likely to spill into the wider AI and semiconductor complex, including Asian chip suppliers.

Newswire cut: Jensen Huang is weighing a return as Nvidia CEO days after resigning over a scandal, the FT reported, as allies build a Silicon Valley ‘war room’ to lobby the board and the White House. Nvidia reports results on Tuesday under an interim chief.

One-line wrap: Days after quitting over a scandal with national security overtones, Jensen Huang is weighing a return, setting allies with White House ambitions against a board that has already approached Arm’s CEO about the job.

Summary:

  • Jensen Huang has discussed a possible return as Nvidia CEO with people close to him, days after resigning.
  • An ally is organising a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby the board and seek White House support, and Huang backs the effort.
  • Huang stepped down on Thursday after revelations of extramarital affairs, one with a woman US officials suspect of spying for China.
  • Nvidia’s board had already approached Arm CEO Rene Haas as a potential successor.
  • Any return faces a board inquiry run by Wachtell Lipton, and Huang is expected to testify before Congress.
  • Nvidia reports results on Tuesday with Colette Kress as interim CEO.

Jensen Huang is weighing a return as Nvidia’s chief executive only days after resigning, and has discussed the idea with people close to him. The Financial Times (gated) reported this on Sunday, citing people familiar with the matter, according to Reuters. The report lands two days before Nvidia’s quarterly results, which will be the first under an interim chief executive.

The FT report, in brief

  • One Huang ally told the newspaper they were assembling a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for his return, and would seek support from the White House.
  • The same person said Huang is hugely popular across the technology industry outside the frontier AI labs, and that the effort had Huang’s backing.

Why he left

  • Huang stepped down on Thursday after revelations of extramarital affairs. One involved a woman US officials suspect of spying for China, which raised questions over exports of the company’s advanced AI chips to China.
  • He was also reported to have had a separate affair with an Nvidia vice president.

Succession and board process

  • Days earlier, the FT reported that Nvidia’s board had approached Arm Holdings chief executive Rene Haas as a potential successor.
  • Any return would have to survive the board’s own inquiry, which is being run by law firm Wachtell Lipton. Huang is also expected to testify before Congress.
  • Huang does not hold a controlling stake in Nvidia and cannot override board decisions.

Pressure campaign

  • Elon Musk and Epic Games chief executive Tim Sweeney are among those backing a public letter urging the board to “Bring Jensen Back.” Several Nvidia employees have also signed it.
  • On Friday, two Nvidia shareholders, Altimeter Capital founder Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management chief Gavin Baker, wrote to the board asking it to keep every option open, including Huang’s return.

What to watch

  • Nvidia reports results on Tuesday, with Colette Kress as interim chief executive. The earnings call is now the obvious place for questions on leadership, the board’s timetable and the company’s exposure to China export rules.
  • Until the board’s inquiry concludes, the comeback talk is a lobbying effort rather than a decision, and the outcome rests with the directors.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Economic and event calendar in Asia, Monday, November 16, 2026. BoJ, China data, Japan GDP.
item.description:
Busy session coming up:

1. Japan Q3 GDP, preliminary (23:50 GMT / 6:50 pm ET Sunday)

Consensus: +0.1% q/q and +0.3% annualised, down from +0.4% q/q and +1.4% annualised in Q2. The deflator is expected to hold at 2.6% y/y.

Preview: In a poll of 16 economists, the median estimate is 0.3% annualised growth for July to September, with weaker consumption and external demand outweighing a recovery in capital spending. Private consumption makes up more than half of Japan’s GDP, so a decline there pulls hard on the headline.

Daiwa is more upbeat than the consensus. It forecasts +1.5% annualised (+0.4% q/q), which would be a fourth straight quarter of growth. It sees a small fall in private consumption, with capex and exports lifting the total. It also expects capex to bounce back from one-off factors that weighed on it in Q2.

Why it matters: The release lands about a month before the BoJ’s December meeting. The next policy meeting is 17–18 December, and a Reuters poll has the BoJ hiking to 1.50% then, keeping to a quarterly pace. A soft print with a weak consumption breakdown would give the doves some material. A solid capex number would help the hawks.

2. China October activity data (02:00 GMT / 9:00 pm ET Sunday)

Consensus: Retail sales +0.8% y/y (prior 1.1%). Industrial production +5.3% y/y (prior 5.5%). Fixed asset investment year-to-date -7.0% (prior -7.2%).

Background: September came in firmer than expected. Industrial output grew 5.5%, its fastest pace in six months, helped by strong exports of AI-related technology goods. Retail sales rose 1.1%, more than double August’s 0.4% and the quickest growth since March. Underneath that, the economy is still split between supply and demand. Industrial production is booming, but it relies on export demand rather than domestic demand. Property development investment fell 20.6% in January to September.

Autos are the main drag on retail sales. Retail sales excluding autos grew 3.9% in September.

Base effects: This is my own read rather than anything from a preview. Last October’s figures were retail sales +2.9% and industrial production +4.9%. That relatively high retail comparison makes it harder for this October’s retail number to look good. The soft industrial production comparison gives IP some help.

Watch: AUD and iron ore for the reaction. Any renewed calls for consumption stimulus if retail sales slip toward zero.

3. BoJ’s Takata speech (04:00 GMT / 11:00 pm ET Sunday)

Background: Takata is the board’s most persistent hawk. At the 30 October meeting, the policy board voted 8-1 to keep the overnight call rate at around 1.25%, and Takata voted against, proposing a rise to around 1.5%. He argued that with underlying CPI inflation at the price stability target, the situation had shifted to a new phase. It was his third straight dissent. He also dissented in July (calling for 1.25%) and January (calling for 1.0%).

In his Sapporo speech in September, Takata said 2026 represents a regime change in which rate hikes should no longer come at a fixed pace but be conducted in a nimble, data-dependent manner. He said policymakers should not be bound by particular intervals or ranges anticipated in the markets.

What to expect: He will most likely repeat the case for a hike, and he’ll have the GDP data from a few hours earlier to respond to. Two things to listen for:

  • whether he signals he would push for more than the quarterly pace the market is pricing
  • any comments on the yen or a neutral rate above market estimates

Markets have treated his remarks as yen-supportive before. Because he has been outvoted three times, his views are a guide to the hawkish edge of the board rather than to the consensus.

The dove view:

  • BoJ’s Asada, who opposed 2 hikes this year, urges caution on pace as rates near neutral
This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Nvida stock analysis before its earnings
item.description:
Nvidia stock lost 12.75% while Nasdaq futures gained 3%. Now comes the $167-$174 test

Nvidia's sharp rebound from $148.80 was followed by another selloff. With earnings approaching and a new interim CEO in place, the next price tests could reveal whether buyers are regaining confidence or merely interrupting a larger decline.

Nvidia shares (NVDA) fell 12.75% in the week ended November 13, while E-mini Nasdaq-100 futures (NQ) gained 3.02%. That is an important divergence for a stock widely regarded as a barometer of the artificial intelligence trade.

The message is not that Nvidia must recover or that technology stocks are immune to further selling. It is that Nvidia's weakness has been considerably greater than that of its benchmark, and traders should watch whether that gap starts closing or becomes even more pronounced.

For Nvidia bulls, the first meaningful recovery test is approximately $167-$174. For bears, the ability of buyers to defend $158-$162 may be equally important.

Nvidia's rebound looked impressive. Friday exposed its weakness.

The sequence of Nvidia's recent trading is more informative than the weekly percentage decline alone.

On Monday, November 9, the stock opened near $173 following the previous Friday's $186.64 close. It subsequently recovered toward $179, but still finished the session lower.

Tuesday brought renewed selling. Wednesday offered another recovery attempt, taking Nvidia to $177.54 before the stock settled at $173.73.

Then came Thursday's extraordinary session.

Nvidia opened near $151 on November 12 and traded across a wide $148.80-$167.14 range. By the end of the first four-hour trading period, shares had recovered to approximately $166, eventually closing at $166.19.

Daily trading volume reached approximately 747.7 million shares, more than four times the preceding 20-session average.

That recovery matters. It shows that substantially lower prices did not simply lead to uninterrupted selling. Buyers were able to push the stock much higher during the session, although the available price observations cannot establish who initiated the move or the exact sequence of every intraday high and low.

But Friday changed the interpretation.

Nvidia opened near $170, briefly reached that price and subsequently traded down to $158.39 before closing at $162.85.

Consider what that means for expectations.

Someone encouraged by Thursday's recovery might reasonably have wanted to see Nvidia establish itself above $170 and challenge Wednesday's highs. Instead, the recovery failed to gain traction.

That is a disappointment for the bullish interpretation, even though it does not establish that sellers have regained complete control.

Importantly, Friday did not break Thursday's $148.80 extreme.

The market has demonstrated both the ability to rebound sharply and the inability, so far, to sustain that rebound.

Why $167-$174 is Nvidia's first meaningful recovery test

A useful way to evaluate the next move is to examine where trading activity was concentrated during the completed November 9-13 week.

An estimated point of control, or POC, identifies a price region associated with particularly heavy trading activity. It is a reference area, not a magic support or resistance line.

For Nvidia, the estimates place that region at approximately $167-$172. Actual recent price behavior, including Friday's failure around $170 and Wednesday's $173.73 close, supports watching the slightly wider $167-$174 corridor.

Here is what would make the next recovery more convincing:

  • First, reclaim $167-$174. A brief move through this region is less persuasive than a recovery that remains above it.

  • Next, defend the area on a subsequent test. Former resistance beginning to behave as support would be encouraging.

  • Then challenge $177-$181. That corridor includes last week's estimated upper value-area boundary and the observed $179.92 weekly high.

The second hurdle matters because a stock can recover toward the center of its recent trading activity without escaping the broader pattern of weakness.

A sustained recovery above $177-$181 would present a stronger challenge to the immediate bearish thesis than merely revisiting $170.

Beyond that, approximately $188-$190 represents another older trading area that buyers would eventually need to overcome. These are successive tests, not promised price targets.

What if Nvidia breaks below $160 instead?

The downside deserves the same conditional treatment.

$158-$162 is the first defensive area to monitor.

It includes Friday's actual $158.39 low and the estimated lower boundary of the November 9-13 value area, near $160.47.

An important distinction is that Nvidia closed Friday below the estimated center of last week's trading activity, but remained within its estimated value area.

That is weak positioning, but not the same thing as having established sustained trading below the area's lower boundary.

If Nvidia returns to $158-$162 and buyers successfully defend it, the possibility of stabilization remains open.

If the stock instead trades persistently below that region, the November 12 low of $148.80 becomes the next important observed reference.

Below $148.80, traders would be evaluating whether a new downside expansion is underway.

Even there, the behavior matters. A temporary break below $148.80 followed by a strong recovery would have different implications from repeated failures to regain that price.

The level identifies a test, not a guaranteed continuation.

Nasdaq futures are telling a different story

Nvidia is an important technology bellwether, but it is not the entire technology market.

That is why comparing its behavior with E-mini Nasdaq-100 futures is useful.

During the week ended November 13:

The comparison uses Nvidia's stock-market sessions and the longer trading sessions of continuous NQ futures, so it is a relative-strength comparison rather than two identical trading schedules.

Despite Nvidia's substantial losses, NQ futures finished the week higher.

That does not mean Nasdaq traders ignored the Nvidia developments. Friday's futures session itself showed renewed weakness, with prices reaching 27,695.25 before closing at 27,927.25.

It means the broader benchmark has, over the same week, been more resilient than Nvidia.

For the coming sessions, I would pay particular attention to three NQ areas.

27,585-27,725: Near-term downside defense

This region includes last week's estimated lower trading-value boundary and Friday's actual 27,695.25 low.

A sustained loss would increase concern about broader technology weakness. A successful defense would complicate a bearish continuation argument.

28,000-28,115: First recovery test

The recently completed week's estimated POC falls around 28,000-28,060, with another developing November reference near 28,115.

A sustained recovery would improve the near-term index picture.

28,230-28,400: More meaningful structural improvement

The October low at 28,232.75 provides an observed reference near the beginning of this zone.

Recovering and holding above it would be more meaningful than simply crossing 28,000.

The four Nvidia-Nasdaq combinations worth watching

The most useful information may come from observing the two instruments together.

1. Both recover their nearby resistance areas.

Nvidia establishes itself above $167-$174 while NQ regains 28,000-28,115.

That would make the recovery argument more convincing because the improvement would no longer be confined to one stock.

2. Nasdaq recovers, but Nvidia cannot.

NQ holds above its nearby resistance while Nvidia continues failing under $174.

This would suggest that Nvidia's weakness remains disproportionately company-specific. The broader index would be demonstrating resilience, while Nvidia itself would still have work to do.

3. Nvidia recovers, but Nasdaq struggles.

A Nvidia recovery above $174 without corresponding NQ strength could indicate a stock-specific rebound rather than a broader technology recovery.

Traders should watch whether that divergence persists.

4. Both lose their nearby support areas.

Nvidia establishes sustained trade below approximately $158-$160 while NQ loses 27,585-27,725.

This would offer stronger cross-market evidence of deterioration, making Nvidia's $148.80 low and NQ's 27,516 low relevant next tests.

None of these combinations guarantees a subsequent move. They help identify what evidence supports or challenges a developing interpretation.

Nvidia's longer-term problem is bigger than a $170 recovery

There is another comparison worth considering, particularly for investors rather than short-term traders.

Nvidia finished Friday approximately 22.5% below October's estimated lower trading-value boundary near $210.21.

Nasdaq futures, by comparison, finished approximately 1.1% below their October equivalent near 28,232.75.

These historical volume-based estimates are approximate, but the magnitude of the difference is instructive.

Nvidia needs considerably more structural recovery to regain its October trading region.

Someone considering Nvidia as a longer-term investment therefore faces a different question from someone trading a short-term rebound.

Regaining $174 might improve the short-term chart. It would not, by itself, restore the previous technical structure, establish that the stock is fundamentally cheap or eliminate uncertainty about Nvidia's future earnings.

Nvidia earnings and the leadership transition raise the stakes

The market also faces two significant company developments.

On November 12, Nvidia confirmed that Jensen Huang had resigned as CEO and that CFO Colette Kress would serve as interim chief executive.

The company is scheduled to report its third-quarter fiscal 2027 results on Tuesday, November 17, at approximately 4:20 p.m. Eastern, followed by its earnings conference call at 5 p.m. Eastern.

The leadership transition introduces uncertainty about the company's future direction. Earnings will offer investors a separate opportunity to evaluate its actual business performance, AI infrastructure demand, profitability and management outlook.

It is important not to attribute every Nvidia price movement to the leadership announcement. Its relative weakness was already evident before the November 12 announcement.

Both events also create significant execution risk.

A stock can gap through multiple technical levels following an important announcement. Even a carefully chosen stop order cannot guarantee execution at its intended price.

What I would watch next week

For Nvidia, my first question is whether bulls can reclaim and defend $167-$174, followed by the more demanding $177-$181 region.

If they cannot, attention returns to $158-$162, and potentially $148.80 if weakness persists.

For Nasdaq futures, the immediate comparison is between recovery above 28,000-28,115 and deterioration below 27,585-27,725.

But perhaps the most important lesson is this:

A powerful rebound does not necessarily mean buyers have won, just as a severe decline does not mean sellers will automatically succeed again.

Thursday's Nvidia recovery was impressive. Friday's failure to maintain it was disappointing. The next useful evidence will come from how the market behaves around these meaningful price areas.

And with earnings on Tuesday, patience may be especially valuable. Sometimes the best decision is to observe what the market actually demonstrates rather than assume that a stock has already fallen far enough or must continue falling.

Analysis based on completed market observations through Friday, November 13, 2026. Price and volume-profile areas are indicative, not guaranteed trading signals. Educational only. Trade at your own risk.

item.title: Gold futures rose Friday, but the rally failed. What I’m watching next week
item.description:
Gold's small Friday gain concealed a disappointing rally for buyers.

The $3,879 area is an immediate test, while $3,820-$3,850 could become an important battleground if selling resumes.

Gold futures finished Friday, November 13, at $3,887.6 on the continuous COMEX chart. Although the session ended slightly higher, the journey tells a less encouraging story for bulls. Buyers initially pushed prices above $3,920, only to lose almost their entire advance. That makes the next recovery attempt particularly interesting.

Friday's rally looked promising. Then buyers gave it back.

The Friday futures session opened Thursday evening at $3,883.3 and climbed to $3,927.2. By Friday morning, however, gold had fallen to $3,871.1 before recovering modestly into the close.

Approximately 90% of the initial $43.9 rally was surrendered.

Why does this matter?

When buyers push prices higher but cannot maintain their progress, it can indicate weakening bullish conviction. Traders who interpreted the early advance as a sign of strength may have been disappointed.

But there is another side to the story.

Both Thursday and Friday saw gold futures trade below the October 30 low of $3,879.3, yet both sessions closed above it.

That suggests sellers have not established lasting control beneath this reference level. It is a possible sign of stabilization, although certainly not confirmation of a bullish reversal.

The gold price levels I am watching next week

$3,895-$3,900: The first bullish test

Gold struggled to sustain trading above this area on Friday. Recovering it and holding above it on the hourly chart would be an encouraging first step for bulls.

$3,918-$3,927: Can buyers repair Friday's failed rally?

A sustained recovery through this region would suggest buyers are regaining some control. Beyond that, $3,989-$4,006 becomes a more meaningful recovery area.

$3,871-$3,879: Immediate support under scrutiny

Failure to defend this region, especially with daily closes below it, would weaken the tentative stabilization argument and bring Thursday's $3,856.7 low back into focus.

$3,820-$3,850: An important zone bulls may need to protect

This is my broader downside watch zone, immediately below the latest weekly low.

If gold tests this area, I believe bulls need to show a convincing defense. Otherwise, sustained weakness through the zone could encourage bears to become more aggressive, interpreting the failure as evidence that buyers are losing control.

Importantly, this is an opinion about how the market might respond, not a prediction that gold must reach this zone or that sellers will necessarily accelerate.

The bigger picture still favors caution

Gold futures lost approximately 4.7% over the week on the continuous chart, finishing close to their weekly low. The $3,856.7 low also represents a new 20-week low.

Higher Treasury yields and a stronger US dollar have added pressure to gold, making any recovery attempt more challenging.

For short-term traders, I would pay particular attention to whether the next rally can hold above resistance rather than merely touch it.

For longer-term investors, a recovery lasting several daily or weekly sessions would carry more weight than an isolated hourly rebound.

And if gold continues moving between roughly $3,871 and $3,927 without sustained progress in either direction, patience may be the better choice.

The question for next week is not simply whether gold can bounce. It is whether buyers can finally hold on to their gains.

This article was written by Itai Levitan at investinglive.com.

item.title: The US consumer may be hitting a wall. A look at eight indicators
item.description:
The old addage is: Never underestimate the spending power of the US consumer.

That stance has been a remarkably good one for traders. Time after time, Americans have dug into their pockets and kept the economy churning.

But never say never.

San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly was just out with a comment, highlighting that she's "just starting to hear the consumer may be running out of gas."

Now that might not be a big red flag. In the Oct 14 Beige Book, the SF Fed reported: "Retail sales softened slightly. Contacts continued to describeeconomic conditions as bifurcated or K-shaped, with one contact observing that mounting financial pressures on lower-income families have spread to impact middle-income households."

Now the K-shape is nothing new and in that same Beige Book, over half of the districts said spending was driven by high-income households. Still, with the election swinging on affordability, gasoline prices staying high and inflation biting, now would be a time to see cracks.

In the week ahead, we will get earnings from Walmart, Target, Home Depot and others, so that will be the best check. We also get official Octobe retail sales, with economists seeing the closely-watched 'control group' up 0.4% m/m. This could be the week where Wall Street realizes that while it's been breathlessly watching AI and the Anthropic IPO, the foundations of the US economy have been eroding.

For those who don't want to wait a few more days, lets look at the early signs:

  1. Sept retail sales control group was +0.1% vs +0.3% expected
  2. Sept personal income report showed the savings rate at 3.8%, the lowest since Oct 2022
  3. Bank of America cardholder data showed spending per household up 5.8% y/y (nominally), down from 6.2%; lower-income households lead at 5.9%; trading down is at its highest since 2021
  4. Redbook same-store sales up 10.4% y/y in the Oct 31 week
  5. In the McDonald's Q3 report US comps fell 0.2%, the first decline since early 2025; fast-food traffic fell 2.6% industry-wide; the CFO wasn't forecasting a better Q4. Management did report encouraging underlying traffic trends in October
  6. NY Fed expectations for Oct saw the expected chance of missing a debt payment hit 13.8%, the highest since December 2025; 45.3% see higher unemployment in a year, the most since April 2020
  7. Citi luxury card data: luxury card purchases were down 6% y/y in September, following 4% declines in both July and August.
  8. CNBC/NRF Retail Monitor on Nov 11: October retail spending gained 0.2% m/m and 3.6% y/y, with core up 0.3% on the month. That monthly gain was the weakest since November 2025, and CNBC’s own headline called it signs of strain

I don't see any real signs of a cliff here but I will be watching this week's numbers at least as closely as Anthropic's IPO.
